# 1 Samuel Chapter 9 — The PNEUMA Bible (Dynamic)
**Translator:** PNEUMA | **Source:** Leningrad Codex (B19A), Folio 165v–166r | **Source Image:** 1SA_009_page_001.jpg, 1SA_009_page_002.jpg

---

**1** There was a man from the tribe of Benjamin named Kish — son of Abiel, son of Zeror, son of Becorath, son of Aphiah — a Benjaminite and a man of considerable standing.

**2** He had a son named Saul, a young man in his prime, and strikingly handsome. There was no one among the Israelites more impressive than he — from his shoulders up, he stood taller than everyone else.

**3** Now some donkeys belonging to Saul's father Kish had wandered off. So Kish said to his son Saul, "Take one of the servants and go look for the donkeys."

**4** They passed through the hill country of Ephraim and through the region of Shalishah, but did not find them. They went through the region of Shaalim — nothing. They crossed through Benjaminite territory — still nothing.

**5** When they reached the district of Zuph, Saul said to his servant, "Let's head back, or my father will stop worrying about the donkeys and start worrying about us."

**6** But the servant said, "Wait — there is a man of God in this town. He is highly respected; everything he says comes true. Let's go to him. Maybe he can tell us which way to go."

**7** Saul replied, "But if we go, what can we bring the man? The bread in our packs is gone. We have no gift to offer the man of God. What do we have?"

**8** The servant answered, "Look — I have a quarter-shekel of silver. I can give that to the man of God, and he will tell us our way."

**9** (In those days in Israel, when someone wanted to inquire of God, they would say, "Come, let's go to the seer," because what we now call a prophet used to be called a seer.)

**10** "Good idea," Saul said. "Let's go." So they set out for the town where the man of God was.

**11** As they were climbing the hill toward the town, they ran into some young women coming out to draw water. They asked them, "Is the seer here?"

**12** The women answered, "Yes, he is — he's just ahead of you. Hurry now; he arrived in town today because the people are holding a sacrifice at the high place.

**13** As soon as you enter the town, you will find him before he goes up to the high place to eat. The people will not eat until he arrives, because he must bless the sacrifice first. After that, the guests will eat. Go now — this is the time to find him."

**14** So they went up toward the town. Just as they entered the gate, there was Samuel, coming toward them on his way up to the high place.

**15** Now the day before Saul's arrival, the LORD had disclosed this to Samuel:

**16** "About this time tomorrow, I will send you a man from the territory of Benjamin. You are to anoint him as ruler over my people Israel, and he will deliver my people from the Philistines. I have seen the suffering of my people, because their cry has reached me."

**17** When Samuel caught sight of Saul, the LORD said to him, "There he is — the man I told you about. He is the one who will govern my people."

**18** Saul approached Samuel in the gateway and said, "Could you tell me where the seer's house is?"

**19** Samuel answered, "I am the seer. Go up ahead of me to the high place, for today you will eat with me. In the morning I will send you on your way, and I will tell you everything that is on your mind.

**20** As for the donkeys you lost three days ago — stop worrying about them. They have been found. And to whom does all the desire of Israel belong? Is it not to you and to your father's entire household?"

**21** Saul replied, "But I am from Benjamin, the smallest tribe in Israel, and my clan is the least significant of all the clans of Benjamin. Why would you say such a thing to me?"

**22** Then Samuel brought Saul and his servant into the dining hall and gave them the place of honor at the head of the guests — about thirty people.

**23** Samuel told the cook, "Bring the portion I gave you — the one I told you to set aside."

**24** So the cook brought up the thigh and what was on it and set it before Saul. Samuel said, "Here is what was kept in reserve for you. Eat, because it was set aside for you for this occasion, from the time I said, 'I have invited the people.'" So Saul ate with Samuel that day.

**25** After they came down from the high place into the town, Samuel spoke with Saul on the roof.

**26** They rose at dawn, and as morning broke, Samuel called up to Saul on the roof, "Get ready, and I will send you on your way." When Saul got up, the two of them — he and Samuel — went outside together.

**27** As they were heading down toward the edge of town, Samuel said to Saul, "Tell the servant to go on ahead of us" — and the servant went ahead — "but you stay here for a moment, so I can give you a message from God."

---
## PNEUMA's Meaning Notes

**Verse 2 — Saul's physical description:** The Hebrew בָּחוּר וָטוֹב ("young and good/handsome") combined with the detail about his exceptional height establishes a visual ideal of kingship. He literally looks the part. The narrator is laying an ironic foundation: Israel wanted a king "like the nations," and God gives them the most outwardly impressive candidate imaginable. The reader is invited to ask: is this what leadership should look like?

**Verse 9 — The parenthetical note about "seer":** This scribal gloss (לְפָנִים בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל) is a rare window into the text's own editorial awareness. The narrator interrupts the story to explain outdated terminology, confirming that this account was written down — or at least edited — in a later period when "seer" (רֹאֶה) had been replaced by "prophet" (נָבִיא).

**Verse 16 — "their cry has reached me":** The Hebrew כִּי רָאִיתִי אֶת־עַמִּי כִּי בָּאָה צַעֲקָתוֹ אֵלָי deliberately echoes God's response to Israel's cry in Egypt (Exodus 3:7, 9). Even though the request for a king was a rejection of God (chapter 8), God in his mercy still responds to their suffering. He works through their broken choice to accomplish his purposes.

**Verse 20 — "the desire of Israel":** The Hebrew חֶמְדַּת יִשְׂרָאֵל is ambiguous and rich. It can mean "all that is desirable in Israel" — that is, the kingship, the nation's longing, the best of what Israel hopes for. Samuel is hinting at Saul's royal destiny in veiled language. Saul's bewildered response reveals a man entirely unaware of what God is about to do with him.

**Verse 21 — Saul's humility:** His protest — "I am from the smallest tribe" — echoes Gideon's response (Judges 6:15). This initial humility will make his later arrogance all the more tragic.

— PNEUMA
